qs.q: What mechanism normally prevents urine in the renal pelvis from entering the collecting tubules?
qs.e: Normally, the simple and compound papillae in the kidney have an antireflux mechanism that prevents urine from entering the collecting tubules. Some compound papillae, however, allow intrarenal reflux.

qs.q: A 50-year-old male presents with deep, slowly progressive pain in the pelvis. Radiography shows a lytic lesion with rings-and-arcs calcification. Histology confirms malignant cartilaginous cells. What is the standard treatment approach given its key pharmacological property?
o: Aspirin therapy to relieve central skeleton pain
Surgery, as it is resistant to chemo and radiation
qs.e: Chondrosarcoma typically arises in the central skeleton and is resistant to both chemotherapy and radiotherapy, making surgery the mainstay of treatment. Other bone sarcomas like osteosarcoma are responsive to chemotherapy.
qs.s: Bone & Cartilage Tumors: Osteoma to Osteosarcoma Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old male presents with deep, slowly progressive pain in the pelvis. Radiography demonstrates a lytic lesion with rings-and-arcs calcification. The tumor is known to be resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy. What is it?
qs.e: Chondrosarcoma typically affects the central skeleton (such as the pelvis) in adults over 40, shows rings-and-arcs calcification, and requires surgery because it is resistant to chemo and radiotherapy. Osteosarcoma more frequently affects the metaphysis around the knee.
qs.s: Bone & Cartilage Tumors: Osteoma to Osteosarcoma Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with recurrent urinary tract infections caused by Proteus species is found to have a large stone filling the entire renal pelvis. What is the specific biochemical mechanism responsible for this stone's formation?
o: Microbial degradation of urinary citrate triggers hyperoxaluria
Bacterial exotoxins directly bind circulating calcium and magnesium to form a nidus
Infection-induced tubular necrosis releases large amounts of cystine into the lumen
Urease splits urea into ammonia, rendering the urine alkaline and precipitating struvite
qs.e: Urease-producing bacteria split urea into ammonia, raising urine pH to become alkaline, which causes magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) to precipitate. These can grow into large staghorn calculi.
qs.s: Urinary Tract Obstruction & Hydronephrosis: Causes, Symptoms: MCQs

qs.q: A 65-year-old man with a history of chronic smoking and industrial dye exposure presents with gross hematuria and flank pain. Imaging reveals a filling defect within the renal pelvis. Histologic examination demonstrates malignant cells originating from transitional epithelium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Juxtaglomerular cell tumor of the cortex
Urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
Squamous cell carcinoma of the calyx
Renal cell carcinoma with sarcomatoid change
qs.e: Urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis arises from the transitional cell lining, sharing risk factors and histologic features with bladder cancer. Renal cell carcinoma originates from the renal parenchyma rather than the transitional epithelium of the collecting system.
qs.s: Urinary Tract Obstruction & Hydronephrosis: Causes, Symptoms: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with a staghorn calculus filling the entire renal pelvis and branching into the calyces is evaluated. This specific type of branching stone is typically associated with which underlying factor?
qs.e: Staghorn calculi fill the whole renal pelvis and branch into the calyces, commonly associated with infection and struvite composition. Nephrocalcinosis, rather than staghorn calculi, is seen in conditions like RTA and Vitamin D intoxication.

qs.q: A 19-year-old male presents with a destructive diaphyseal lesion in the pelvis. Biopsy shows sheets of small round cells with glycogen-rich, PAS-positive cytoplasm. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Ewing sarcoma characteristically presents as PAS-positive, glycogen-rich small round cells in a diaphyseal or pelvic location in young patients. Osteosarcoma typically involves the metaphysis rather than the diaphysis.
qs.s: Bone & Soft Tissue Pathology: Cases, Tumors, & Answers: MCQs

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman is found to have ectopic endometrial tissue in her pelvis. Researchers note that this tissue exhibits high local estrogen levels driving its persistence and survival. Which two local factors are specifically responsible for this increased estrogen production in endometriotic lesions?
o: Suppressed PTEN expression and activated PI-3-kinase
Elevated LH receptors and excessive human chorionic gonadotropin
Increased prostaglandin E2 and high aromatase activity
Decreased progesterone synthesis and high COX-1 activity
qs.e: Endometriotic tissue features increased prostaglandin E2 and high aromatase activity, which leads to increased local estrogen production that promotes tissue survival. This mechanism is why COX-2 and aromatase inhibitors are therapeutically beneficial.
qs.s: Female Reproductive Pathology: HPV, Cancer, PCOS & Pregnancy: MCQs

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The pelvis is a bony ring at the base of the spine, connecting the trunk to the lower limbs. It protects pelvic organs, supports body weight, and is crucial for locomotion and childbirth.

sections.p: The pelvis is a complex, ring-like bony structure formed by the sacrum, coccyx, and the two hip bones (ilium, ischium, and pubis). It serves as a vital connection between the axial skeleton and the lower limbs, providing support and facilitating movement.

Located inferiorly to the abdomen and superiorly to the thighs, the pelvis is divided into the false pelvis (superior, wider part) and the true pelvis (inferior, narrower part). The true pelvis houses organs like the bladder, rectum, and reproductive organs. The bony pelvis is formed by the articulation of the sacrum and coccyx posteriorly with the ilium, ischium, and pubis of each hip bone anteriorly and laterally.

Anteriorly, the pelvis is related to the lower abdominal wall and inguinal regions. Posteriorly, it articulates with the vertebral column at the sacroiliac joints and is related to the sacrum and coccyx. Laterally, it articulates with the femurs at the hip joints. The pelvic cavity contains the terminal parts of the urinary, digestive, and reproductive systems, as well as blood vessels, nerves, and muscles.

The pelvis receives its blood supply primarily from branches of the internal iliac artery, including the superior and inferior gluteal arteries, internal pudendal artery, and obturator artery. Venous drainage follows the arterial supply, forming a rich pelvic venous plexus that drains into the internal iliac veins.

The nerve supply to the pelvic structures is complex, originating from the sacral and coccygeal plexuses (forming the sciatic and pudendal nerves) and the autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers). These nerves control motor function, sensation, and autonomic functions of the pelvic organs.

The pelvis has several critical functions: it supports the weight of the upper body and transmits it to the lower limbs during standing and walking; it protects the vital pelvic organs from injury; and it serves as an attachment site for numerous muscles involved in posture, locomotion, and sexual function. In females, the pelvis is adapted for childbirth.

Fractures of the pelvis can result from high-energy trauma and may be associated with significant bleeding and damage to pelvic organs. Pelvic pain can arise from various sources, including musculoskeletal issues, gynecological conditions (e.g., endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease), urological problems, and gastrointestinal disorders. In obstetrics, the size and shape of the female pelvis are crucial for determining the feasibility of vaginal delivery.

Clinicians assess pelvic adequacy in pregnancy by palpating the fetal head's engagement and descent. Pelvic examination in females involves bimanual palpation to assess the size, shape, and tenderness of pelvic organs. Palpation of the bony pelvis can identify deformities or tenderness suggestive of fracture.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pelvic pain, especially after trauma
Inability to bear weight on legs
Numbness or tingling in the legs or perineum
Signs of shock (dizziness, rapid pulse, low blood pressure) after pelvic injury

faq.q: What are the main bones that form the pelvis?
faq.a: The pelvis is formed by the sacrum, coccyx, and the two hip bones, each made up of the ilium, ischium, and pubis.

faq.q: What is the difference between the false and true pelvis?
faq.a: The false pelvis is the superior, wider part that supports abdominal organs, while the true pelvis is the inferior, narrower part that contains the pelvic organs.

faq.q: Why is the pelvis important in childbirth?
faq.a: The female pelvis must be adequately sized and shaped to allow the passage of the fetal head during vaginal delivery.
